notes: Second full audit, covering everything since feeb9a8 (rounds 2-5) and the first push to GitHub. Static Next.js export: no backend, no auth, no forms, no database, no payments, no AI calls, no analytics. Checked: (1) secrets: none in the working tree or in git history (no .env, key, certificate or credential file was ever committed); .gitignore hardened before the push to cover keys/certificates (*.pem *.key *.crt *.p12 *.pfx *.jks), credential files (.npmrc .netrc *credentials* service-account*.json), host tooling (.vercel .wrangler .netlify .aws .terraform, *.tfstate) and editor/OS noise; no tracked file is caught by the new rules. (2) injection: the only dangerouslySetInnerHTML is components/seo/JsonLd.tsx, which escapes < before serialising; no eval, no new Function, no innerHTML; the six client components (lyrics dialog, lightbox, copy-email, two embed facades, language switcher) render server-passed children and never build markup from strings. (3) content validation: every URL in content/ now goes through httpUrl (zod, protocol pinned to http/https); SiteSchema.url was the one field still on bare z.url(), which in zod 4 accepts javascript: and data:, and is now pinned as well; gallery keys are constrained to /^[a-z0-9-]+$/ and checked against the image manifest at build. (4) deployment: public/_headers keeps CSP (script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline', unavoidable for a static export that inlines RSC payloads; no unsafe-eval; frame-src limited to youtube-nocookie.com and bandcamp.com; object-src none; base-uri self; form-action self; frame-ancestors none), HSTS preload, nosniff, X-Frame-Options DENY, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP; the stale 'no eval needed for three.js' note was corrected since three.js is gone; the production build emits no browser source maps and only out/ is deployed. (5) CI: both workflows now declare least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN scopes (contents: read for CI, permissions: {} for the weekly rebuild); the Cloudflare deploy hook is read from a repository secret into an env var and never echoed. (6) third parties: YouTube and Bandcamp load only after a click, nothing is stored, external links carry rel=noopener. (7) dependencies: npm audit reports 0 vulnerabilities in production dependencies; 7 advisories remain in dev-only tooling (extract-zip, qs, tmp, uuid, via the lighthouse and serve chains), none reachable at runtime and none fixable without a breaking change. Findings: no Critical, no High. Medium: SiteSchema.url accepted any URL scheme (fixed). Low: unconstrained gallery image keys (fixed), unscoped workflow token permissions (fixed), CSP relies on 'unsafe-inline' for scripts (documented, inherent to static export), the booking address is published in plain text in the Impressum (required by German law, accepted), dev-dependency advisories to revisit at the next tooling update. Round 6 delta audit (hero player, painted dividers, retimed background): the one new surface is components/music/HeroPlayer.tsx, a third client component embedding Bandcamp. Its iframe URL is assembled only from content/site.json heroTrack.bandcampTrackId, which the schema pins to /^\d+$/, so nothing user-supplied can reach the src; the release slug is a slug regex and the title is cross-checked at build against that record's own tracklist. The embed origin https://bandcamp.com is already the only Bandcamp host in the CSP frame-src allowlist, the frame carries referrerPolicy strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and nothing is requested before an explicit click with the consent line and a link to the privacy policy shown first. The divider assets (rule-brush.webp, edge-deckle.webp and its mirror) are static images generated from the sleeve and are used only as CSS masks. No new dependency, no new network origin, no new form, storage or script. Findings: no Critical, no High, no Medium. Low: the Bandcamp iframe carries no sandbox attribute, matching the existing Bandcamp and YouTube facades; it loads only on consent from an allowlisted origin, and tightening it would need testing against the player's own requirements. Round 8 delta audit (GitHub Pages deployment). New file .github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml. (1) Permissions are least-privilege per job: build has contents:read plus pages:write and id-token:write, deploy has only pages:write and id-token:write; nothing has contents:write. The build job needs pages:write solely for configure-pages' enablement call. (2) No script injection: the step that derives the base path reads $GITHUB_REPOSITORY as a shell environment variable rather than interpolating ${{ }} inside a run block, which is the injection vector. (3) Triggers are push-on-main and workflow_dispatch only; there is no pull_request or pull_request_target trigger, so no fork can run it. (4) No secrets are referenced. (5) Only first-party actions/* are used. (6) The three build variables are NEXT_PUBLIC_* by design: they are public URLs, and nothing secret is inlined. (7) The published artifact is out/, the same public static site; the preview is deliberately noindex (robots.txt disallows all, every page carries robots: noindex) so it cannot compete with brickwater.de. Findings: no Critical, no High. Medium: GitHub Pages sends no custom headers, so the CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy in public/_headers do not apply to the preview; this is a real loss of defence in depth versus the Cloudflare target, accepted because the preview is a static site with no cookies, no storage, no forms, no auth and no third-party script before an explicit click, and it is documented in GO-LIVE.md section 6. Low: actions are pinned to major tags rather than commit SHAs, consistent with the repo's existing workflows. Follow-up audit of 113c7a2, which moved the three Pages build variables from job scope to the build step. The derived values now go to $GITHUB_OUTPUT instead of $GITHUB_ENV and are read back as step outputs inside an `env:` mapping, never spliced into a `run:` shell body, which is the placement that makes a ${{ }} expression an injection vector; the values themselves still come from $GITHUB_REPOSITORY via shell parameter expansion, and that variable is GitHub-controlled and cannot contain a newline, so it cannot forge extra output lines. No permission, action or secret changed. The change is a strict reduction in blast radius: the build variables no longer reach `npm ci` or `npm run check`. Findings: no Critical, no High, no Medium. Third audit of the Pages workflow, after Pages turned out to be served from the gh-pages branch rather than from an Actions artifact. The workflow now builds and force-pushes the output to that branch, which needs a token that can write to the repository. That is a real permission increase and it is contained deliberately: `build` keeps contents:read and is the only job that runs `npm ci`, while `publish` holds contents:write, downloads the artifact and runs nothing from node_modules, so third-party install scripts never share a job with the write token. pages:write and id-token:write are gone. The push is a force-push with an explicit HEAD:gh-pages refspec, so it cannot touch main or any tag, and a guard aborts if the artifact has no index.html, so a broken build cannot blank the site. The token is passed through an `env:` mapping and read back as a shell variable rather than interpolated into the script body. Triggers are still push-on-main and workflow_dispatch only, so no fork can run it. Only first-party actions/* are used. Findings: no Critical, no High. Medium: the publish job can write to the repository, accepted with the isolation above. Low: actions are pinned to major tags rather than commit SHAs. Round 8 delta audit. The only security-sensitive change is a `schedule:` cron trigger added to .github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml so the live preview rebuilds weekly and past concerts retire on their own; a static export decides which shows are upcoming at build time, so nothing else would. A scheduled run executes the workflow file from the default branch with the same job permissions already audited (build has contents:read and runs npm, publish has contents:write and runs no third-party code), adds no secret, no action and no new trigger surface a fork can reach. Everything else in this round is markup, CSS, copy and documentation. Findings: no Critical, no High, no Medium. Operational note, not a finding: GitHub disables scheduled workflows on a public repository after 60 days without activity, so the weekly rebuild stops if the repo goes untouched that long. Round 9 delta audit, covering the new .github/workflows/deploy-goneo.yml, which is the first workflow in this repository to handle real server credentials, and public/.htaccess. (1) Credential isolation is the main control and it holds: the `build` job runs npm ci and the build with contents:read and no secrets; the `publish` job holds GONEO_HOST, GONEO_USER and GONEO_PASSWORD, installs only lftp from apt and executes nothing from node_modules, so a compromised dependency cannot reach the server. Verified by parsing the file: build has secrets=false/npm=true, publish has secrets=true/npm=false. (2) Trigger surface is workflow_dispatch and schedule only. No pull_request or pull_request_target, so a fork can never obtain the secrets. (3) Log hygiene: the password is passed as LFTP_PASSWORD and consumed by lftp's --env-password, so it never appears on a command line or in the process table; lftp runs with cmd:trace off; no shell tracing anywhere. (4) The upload is a destructive mirror with --delete, guarded four ways: production requires the literal word deploy in a confirm input, the remote path must be a configured non-empty value, the artifact is rejected unless it contains both index.html and .htaccess, and the remote directory is listed and the run aborts if it looks like an account root (mail, logs, .ssh) rather than a document root. (5) A backup of the remote directory is deliberately NOT uploaded as a workflow artifact: this repository is public and artifacts of public repositories are downloadable by anyone, so capturing a server directory into one could publish whatever it holds. Restore is goneo's own backup, documented in GO-LIVE.md. (6) public/.htaccess restores the full header set that Cloudflare gets from _headers and that GitHub Pages cannot send at all; every block is wrapped in <IfModule> because an unguarded directive from an unloaded module is a 500 on every request, and this file is uploaded to a server whose module list we do not control. Findings: no Critical, no High. Medium: the SFTP host key is accepted unverified (sftp:auto-confirm yes), so a first-connection man-in-the-middle could capture the credentials; on ephemeral runners this is accept-always rather than trust-on-first-use, and it should be replaced with a pinned fingerprint once the key is known. Low: a misconfigured GONEO_PRODUCTION_PATH could still mirror into the wrong directory, which the listing guard reduces but does not eliminate, and actions are pinned to major tags rather than commit SHAs. Round 10 delta audit, covering the goneo workflow correction and the logo assets. The only change to a security-sensitive file is the SFTP port: goneo listens on 2222 rather than the protocol default, so both lftp connections now carry it, sourced from an optional GONEO_PORT variable that defaults to 2222. A port is not a secret and is deliberately a variable rather than one. No permission, trigger, action or credential handling changed, and the credential-isolation split between the build and publish jobs is untouched. The remaining files in this round are the artist's logo and the generator that prepares it, which read a local image and write image assets: no network, no environment beyond the existing build variables, no secrets. Findings: no Critical, no High, no Medium. The SFTP host key is still accepted unverified, already recorded in the previous entry and unchanged here.
